```{r libraries}
if (!requireNamespace("pacman", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pacman")
}
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,  # covers dplyr, ggplot2, lubridate, tidyr, stringr, purrr, forcats
  statmod, tweedie, car,
  glue, broom, janitor
)
train <- read.csv("data/train_outlier.csv")
```


```{r}
train |> 
  summarize(
    n_total = n(),
    n_zero = sum(total_losses = 0),
    pct_zero = glue("{round(mean(total_losses == 0) * 100, 2)}%"),
    mean_losses = round(mean(total_losses), 2),
    var_losses = round(var(total_losses), 2)
  )
```

Estimate `p` using profile likelihood

```{r}
p_profile <- tweedie.profile(
  total_losses ~ 1,
  p.vec = seq(1.1, 1.9, by = 0.1),
  data = train,
  do.plot = TRUE,
  method = "series"
)
```
```{r}
p_optimal <- p_profile$p.max
glue("Optimal Tweedie p: {p_optimal}")
```
```{r}
p_refined <- tweedie.profile(
  total_losses ~ 1,
  p.vec = seq(p_optimal - 0.1, p_optimal + 0.1, by = 0.01),
  data = train,
  do.plot = TRUE,
  method = "series"
)
```
```{r}
p_final = p_refined$p.max
saveRDS(p_final, "tweedie_p.rds")
glue("Tweedie p = {p_final} saved to tweedie_p.rds")
```
# Convert all categorical variables to factors

```{r}
p_final <- readRDS("tweedie_p.rds")
```


```{r}
cat_cols <- c("policy.NBRB","pet.Type",
              "pet.Group","pet.Breed","pet.Gender","pet.Offspring","pet.Microchip","pet.Origin",
              "owner.Gender","owner.Location","owner.Channel"
              )
train <- train |> 
  mutate(across(all_of(cat_cols), factor))
  mutate(
    pet.Type = relevel(pet.Type, ref = "Dog"),
    pet.Group = relevel(pet.Group, ref = "Shorthair"),
    pet.Gender = relevel(pet.Gender, ref = "Male"),
    pet.Offspring = relevel(pet.Offspring, ref = "No"),
    pet.Microchip = relevel(pet.Microchip, ref = "Yes"),
    pet.Origin = relevel(pet.Origin, ref = "Store"),
    pet.Origin = relevel(pet.Origin, ref = "Store"),
    owner.Gender = relevel(owner.Gender, ref = "Male"),
    owner.Location = relevel(owner.Location, ref = "Suburban"),
    policy.NBRB = relevel(policy.NBRB, ref = "RB")
  )
```

We omit pet.Breed from the baseline model because it has a very high dimensionality which would
lead to overfitting and will surely (in its raw form) not be part of the final model.

We also omit pet.Type for exact multicollinearity with pet.Group. Since each level of pet.Group
is strictly nested within either Cat or Dog, including both will cause an exact rank-deficiency singularity.

```{r}
model_A <- glm(
  total_losses ~ pet.Group + pet.Age + pet.Gender + pet.Height +
    pet.Weight + pet.Offspring + pet.Microchip + pet.Origin + owner.Age + owner.Gender +
    owner.Location + owner.CreditScore + owner.Channel + owner.PetCount + policy.NBRB +
    offset(log(policy.Exposure)),
  data = train,
  family = tweedie(var.power = p_final, link.power = 0))
```

# Baseline model summary

```{r}
summary(model_A)
```

```{r}
tidy(model_A) |> 
  mutate(
    coefficient = round(estimate ,4),
    relativity = round(exp(estimate),4),
    pct_change = ifelse(term=="(Intercept)", NA, round((relativity - 1)*100,2))
  ) |> 
  arrange(p.value) |> 
  select(term, coefficient, relativity, pct_change, p.value)
```


Core rating drivers:

- `pet.Age` (t = 60.0, p -> 0): The single largest risk driver. Expected losses increase by approx 23.6% (exp(0.212) - 1) per additional year of age.
- `policy.NBRB` (t = 10.8, p -> 0): New Business (NB) exhibits approx 39.6% higher losses than Renewal Business (RB). Underwriting selection.
- `pet.Gender` (t = -7.3, p < 0.0001): Females have approx 20.2% lower losses than males.
- `owner.PetCount` (t = 7.3, p < 0.0001): Pure premium increases approx 10.2% per additional pet owned.
- `pet.Height` & `pet.Weight` (p ≤ 0.001): Both are significant positive cost drivers capturing physical size and build.
- `pet.Group` (p < 0.05): Dog groups (Working, Sporting, Herding, Hound, Non-Sporting, Terrier) show substantial positive relativities relative to the
  Shorthair cat baseline.
  
Borderline Variables:

- `pet.Offspring` (p = 0.18)

```{r}
glue("
     Null Deviance\t\t: {round(model_A$null.deviance,2)}
     Residual Deviance\t: {round(model_A$deviance,2)} 
     AIC \t\t\t: {round(tweedie_AIC(model_A),2)} 
     Degrees of Freedom\t: {model_A$df.residual} 
     % Deviance explained\t: {round((1- model_A$deviance / model_A$null.deviance)*100, 2)}%
     ")
```

```{r}
alias(model_A)
```

```{r}
vif_results <- vif(model_A)
round(vif_results, 3)
```
```{r}
saveRDS(model_A, "model_A.rds")
write_csv(train, "data/train_modela.csv")
```

```{r}
p_final <- readRDS("tweedie_p.rds")
model_A <- readRDS("model_A.rds")
train<- read_csv("data/train_modela.csv")
```

# Variable Selection

We use `drop1` with the Chi-square test to iteratively remove non-significant variables, then check VIF on the resulting model to identify any remaining multicollinearity concerns.

## Initial drop1

Run `drop1` on the baseline model to assess the contribution of each variable. We remove the least significant variable first and repeat.

```{r}
(d <- drop1(model_A, test = "Chisq"))
tidy(d) |>  select(term, p.value) |> arrange(desc(p.value))
```

## Iterative Variable Removal

Remove the least significant variable identified by `drop1` and refit until all remaining variables have p-values below 0.05.

```{r}
# Implement Backward selection
backward_selection <- function(base_model = model_A, threshold = 0.05){
  print(glue("{strrep('=',100)}"))
  print(glue("Backward selection: Remove least significant variables until remaining have p-values < {threshold}"))
  print(glue("{strrep('=',100)}"))
  
  model_current <- base_model
  
  # Iteration zero
  n_round <- 0 
  print(d <- drop1(model_current, test = "Chisq"))
  print(td <- tidy(d) |>  select(term, p.value) |> arrange(desc(p.value)) |> mutate(p.value = round(p.value,3)) |> head())
  lowest_p <- td[[1,2]]
  
  while(lowest_p > threshold){
    print(glue("{strrep('=',50)}"))
    print(glue("Round {n_round <- n_round+1 } - remove {td[[1,1]]} (p = {lowest_p})"))
    print(glue("{strrep('=',50)}"))
    model_current <- update(model_current, as.formula(glue(". ~ . - {td[[1,1]]}")))
    print(d <- drop1(model_current, test = "Chisq"))
    print(td <- tidy(d) |>  select(term, p.value) |> arrange(desc(p.value)) |> mutate(p.value = round(p.value,3)) |> head())
    lowest_p <- td[[1,2]]
  }
  
  return(model_current)
}

```

```{r}
model_B <- backward_selection()
```

# Feature Generation & Candidate Models

In this section, we test feature transformations and interactions identified during EDA (`3.eda.Rmd`) against `model_B` to find candidate models that improve pure premium estimation. We test raw vs binned forms, polynomial terms, and interaction effects, using AIC as the primary evaluation criterion.

## Helper Function for Model Comparison

We define a reusable function to compare two model formulas by AIC using `tweedie_AIC()`.

```{r}
compare_aic <- function(formula_1, formula_2, label_1, label_2, data, p) {
  m1 <- glm(as.formula(paste(formula_1, collapse = " ")), 
            data = data, family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = p, link.power = 0))
  m2 <- glm(as.formula(paste(formula_2, collapse = " ")), 
            data = data, family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = p, link.power = 0))
  aic1 <- tweedie_AIC(m1)
  aic2 <- tweedie_AIC(m2)
  data.frame(
    model     = c(label_1, label_2),
    AIC       = round(c(aic1, aic2), 2),
    preferred = c(ifelse(aic1 < aic2, "YES", ""),
                  ifelse(aic2 < aic1, "YES", ""))
  )
}
```

## Define the Base Formula

We define the formula from `model_B` as the baseline string for all subsequent feature tests.

```{r}
base_formula <- "total_losses ~ pet.Group + pet.Age + pet.Gender + pet.Height + pet.Weight + owner.PetCount + policy.NBRB + offset(log(policy.Exposure))"
base_formula
```

## Step 1: Raw vs Binned Predictors

In EDA, `owner.PetCount` was binned into an ordinal factor (`1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `5+`) due to thin exposure at high pet counts. We compare the raw linear term against the binned factor.

```{r}
train <- train |>
  mutate(
    pet_count_band = factor(
      ifelse(owner.PetCount >= 5, "5+", as.character(owner.PetCount)),
      levels = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5+")
    )
  )

compare_aic(
  base_formula,
  gsub("owner.PetCount", "pet_count_band", base_formula),
  "Raw: owner.PetCount (Linear)",
  "Binned: pet_count_band (1, 2, 3, 4, 5+)",
  train, p_final
)
```

Linear `owner.PetCount` yields a lower AIC (163,331.6 vs 163,337.9) and consumes fewer degrees of freedom. We retain the raw linear form.


## Step 2: Polynomial Terms (Non-Linear Effects)

EDA revealed that pure premium escalates non-linearly with `pet.Age`, especially in senior years (ages 13+). We test adding a quadratic term `I(pet.Age^2)`.

```{r}
formula_age_sq <- paste0(base_formula, " + I(pet.Age^2)")

compare_aic(
  base_formula,
  formula_age_sq,
  "Linear Age",
  "Linear + Quadratic Age (Age^2)",
  train, p_final
)
```

We also compare Option 1 (Quadratic Polynomial `I(pet.Age^2)`) directly against Option 3 (Non-Linear Size Interaction `pet.Age:pet.Weight`):

```{r}
formula_age_weight <- paste0(base_formula, " + pet.Age:pet.Weight")

compare_aic(
  formula_age_sq,
  formula_age_weight,
  "Option 1: Quadratic Age (Age^2)",
  "Option 3: Age x Weight Interaction",
  train, p_final
)
```

Option 1 (`I(pet.Age^2)`) produces a significantly lower AIC (163,290.5 vs 163,329.1). We retain Option 1 as our best formula.

```{r}
best_formula <- formula_age_sq
best_formula
```

## Step 3: Interaction Terms from EDA

### 3.1 Morphology & Build Density (`pet.Height` x `pet.Weight`)

EDA showed that weight relative to height captures body build density / BMI (e.g., a 20-inch dog weighing 70 lbs vs 25 lbs). We test the interaction `pet.Height:pet.Weight`.

```{r}
formula_morphology <- paste0(best_formula, " + pet.Height:pet.Weight")

compare_aic(
  best_formula,
  formula_morphology,
  "Without Height:Weight",
  "With Height:Weight",
  train, p_final
)
```

The morphology interaction term yields a dramatic reduction in AIC of 41.8 points (163,248.7 vs 163,290.5). We update the best formula.

```{r}
best_formula <- formula_morphology
best_formula
```

### 3.2 Species-Specific Aging (`pet.Age` x `pet.Type`)

EDA lines 810–862 demonstrated that dogs and cats exhibit different aging curve slopes. We test adding `pet.Age:pet.Type`.



```{r}
formula_age_type <- paste0(best_formula, " + pet.Age:pet.Type")

compare_aic(
  best_formula,
  formula_age_type,
  "Without Age:Type",
  "With Age:Type",
  train, p_final
)
```

While biologically sound, `pet.Age:pet.Type` does not improve AIC once `I(pet.Age^2)` and `pet.Height:pet.Weight` are present (163,249.9 vs 163,248.7). We exclude it in favor of parsimony. Possibly because a large portion of deviance that could have been explained by this interaction is already being explained
by `pet.Group`.

### 3.3 High-Divergence Outlier Breed Rating (`breed_outlier`)

In `3.eda.Rmd` (lines 673–749), our dumbbell plot analysis identified 24 high-volume breeds with extreme divergence (>50–60%) from their parent group benchmark pure premium. Out of these 24 outlier breeds, 23 are dogs (plus 1 hybrid cat, Chausie).

Rather than expanding `pet.Breed` into 237 unconstrained dummy variables (which risks severe overfitting), we consolidate these outlier breeds into a parsimonious 3-tier factor (`Standard`, `Surcharge`, `Discount`), consuming only 2 degrees of freedom:

```{r}
# Top 24 outlier breeds identified in 3.eda.Rmd dumbbell plot
surcharge_breeds <- c(
  "Poodle", "Airedale Terrier", "Afghan Hound", "Bull Terrier", "Chausie",
  "Kerry Blue Terrier", "Welsh Springer Spaniel", "Chow Chow", 
  "Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier", "American Staffordshire Terrier", "Pointer", 
  "Polish Lowland Sheepdog", "Collie", "Staffordshire Bull Terrier", 
  "Black and Tan Coonhound", "Dalmatian"
)

discount_breeds <- c(
  "Australian Terrier", "Pumi", "Shetland Sheepdog", "Beagle", 
  "Pyrenean Shepherd", "Pembroke Welsh Corgi", "Rat Terrier", "Norfolk Terrier"
)

train <- train |>
  mutate(
    breed_outlier = factor(
      case_when(
        pet.Breed %in% surcharge_breeds ~ "Surcharge",
        pet.Breed %in% discount_breeds  ~ "Discount",
        TRUE ~ "Standard"
      ),
      levels = c("Standard", "Surcharge", "Discount")
    )
  )

formula_outliers <- paste0(best_formula, " + breed_outlier")

compare_aic(
  best_formula,
  formula_outliers,
  "Without Outlier Breeds (Model D)",
  "With Outlier Breed Tier (Model E)",
  train, p_final
)
```

## Step 4: Summary of Candidate Models

We fit and compare all candidate models representing each modeling stage:

```{r}
model_C <- glm(as.formula(formula_age_sq), data = train, family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = p_final, link.power = 0))
model_D <- glm(as.formula(formula_morphology), data = train, family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = p_final, link.power = 0))
model_E <- glm(as.formula(formula_outliers), data = train, family = statmod::tweedie(var.power = p_final, link.power = 0))

candidate_models <- list(
  "Model A (Full Baseline)"               = model_A,
  "Model B (Selected Main Effects)"       = model_B,
  "Model C (+ Quadratic Age)"             = model_C,
  "Model D (+ Morphology Interaction)"    = model_D,
  "Model E (+ Outlier Breed Rating Tier)" = model_E
)

candidate_comparison <- tibble(
  Model = names(candidate_models),
  AIC = sapply(candidate_models, function(m) round(tweedie_AIC(m), 2)),
  Residual_Deviance = sapply(candidate_models, function(m) round(m$deviance, 1)),
  Pct_Dev_Explained = sapply(candidate_models, function(m) paste0(round((1 - m$deviance / m$null.deviance) * 100, 2), "%")),
  Parameters = sapply(candidate_models, function(m) length(coef(m))),
  Delta_AIC = sapply(candidate_models, function(m) round(tweedie_AIC(m) - tweedie_AIC(model_A), 2))
)

candidate_comparison
```

```

```

```{r}

saveRDS(model_D, "model_D.rds")
saveRDS(model_E, "model_E.rds")

```
